newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian markets head higher to note of caution.
newsitem.headline: Asian markets head higher to note of caution.

text.p: Asian stocks closed mostly higher on Friday, but analysts said many of the gains were technically based and cautioned that consolidation was possible in the week ahead.

Tokyo was the day's star performer, with the Nikkei average soaring 429.93 points or 2.07 percent to end at 21,201.04. However, brokers said the rises were mainly due to futures-linked buying and added that the launch of a new Japanese administration was not a major factor in the market.

"Today's rally had nothing to do with politics. The political factor is neutral (to the market) for now," said Haruyoshi Mabuchi, chief strategist at Nikko Research Centre. "The market will want to see what sort of policies the new government comes up with. If there are no effective policies, that would discourage the market."
Hong Kong stocks capped a record-breaking week with modest gains as investors took heart from the market's firm tone despite some profit-taking today.
The Hang Seng index closed 15.90 points higher at 12,751.16 after falling to a low of 12,667.71 during the session. Turnover was HK$8.42 billion compared to Thursday's HK$10.86 billion.
"Investors are having a hard time understanding the truth that the market needs a period of consolidation," said Kent Rossiter, institutional sales manager at Nikko Securities.
Rory McAllister at HSBC James Capel agreed with this assessment, but added: "The flows are still quite good coming in from overseas. I don't think we have reached the top yet."

Jakarta shares breached the pyschological 600-point barrier on continued foreign-led buying of Telkom and other blue-chips, with the composite index rising 7.43 points, or 1.25 percent, to 602.02 at the close.
"I expect the market to make further gains in the coming week. There could be few a corrections, but positive economic data on Indonesia has led to fresh buying," a foreign broker said.
Thai stocks advanced further, after posting gains in the morning. The SET Index ended up 15.12 points, or 1.59 percent, at 967.60, with telecommunications shares in heavy demand.
In Malaysia, a rebound in heavyweight Tenaga Nasional stock helped push Kuala Lumpur's composite index up 1.67 points to 1,179.60, but dealers said interest was mainly focused on secondary stocks.
Singapore's Straits Times industrials index shrugged off weak economic data, ending at 2,117.23, up 14.50 points, while Australia's all ordinaries index added 15.4 points to close at 2,362.1.
Philippine shares rose for the eighth straight session which saw Manila's composite index put on 26.94 points to 3,090.
Taiwan bucked the trend, with the weighted index losing 47.72 points to 6,581.96 on a lack of fresh news.

Prior to losses on Thursday and Friday, the market had gained nearly 300 points in one week after the government freed one major state fund to invest in stocks and relaxed the investment cap for another.
Korea and New Zealand were also lower, with Seoul's KOSPI index shedding early gains to close 2.65 points lower at 739.11, and Wellington's Top 40 easing 4.00 to 2,334.89.
The dollar was steady in late Tokyo trade, although the mood was nervous in the aftermath of its sharp dive on Thursday triggered by an influential Finance Ministry official's remarks.
At 1203 GMT the dollar was quoted at 112.01/11 yen and 1.5106/11 marks.
Hong Kong gold lurched higher to close at US$378.90/379.40 an ounce against New York's US$378.75/379.25 close on Thursday, but traders said sentiment as "distinctly confused".

SIMEX Brent crude was firmer, supported by stronger oil product prices and technical buying. December Brent was last traded at $22.40 per barrel, up 19 cents compared with London dealings on Thursday when the contract rose six cents to $22.21.
